extracted.intended_audience: general 19th-century magazine readership; educators and prospective female teachers / school superintendents
extracted.subtask_description: A notice/advertisement listing the personal, moral, and academic qualifications desired for hiring a lady as a teacher in public schools, plus the subjects in which applicants will be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired personal and professional qualifications for lady teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'When employing a lady as teacher in our Public Schools, we desire, in addition to a thorough education, to secure the following qualifications; 1st. Ease of address, modest and attractive personal appearance, and habits of neatness and order. 2d. A uniformly kind and generous disposition, entire self-control, with unyielding perseverance and energy. 3d. A spirit of concession and adaptability, that will enable her to conform to the general rules and regulations of the schools, and to harmonize her plans and efforts with those of the other teachers. 4th. A moral and religious character, that will cause her to feel the full responsibility of her position, and make her guard with a watchful eye the habits and principles of the children under her charge. 5th. Such dignity of person and manners as will secure the deference of pupils, and the respect and confidence of parents. A freedom, both from girlish frivolities, and old-maidish crabbedness and prudery. 6th. Correct social habits, a well cultivated literary taste, and a mind richly stored with general information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advertisement frames these as essential in addition to a thorough education. The editor's commentary immediately following questions the realism of expecting all these perfections in one person ('Where, oh, where is she?'), noting that such an expectation presumes a wealthy community able to secure such a paragon. Use this list as idealized hiring standards, but be aware the page criticizes them as likely unattainable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects of examination for teacher applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants for places as teachers in our Public Schools will be examined in the following branches of study, or others, the study of which would furnish an equal amount of mental discipline: Arithmetic, Algebra, Geometry, Mensuration, Trigonometry, Mechanical Philosophy, Geography, Physiology, Zoology, Natural Philosophy, Meteorology, Botany, Chemistry, Geology, Astronomy, Orthography, Reading, Penmanship, English Grammar, History, Bookkeeping, Political Science, Moral Science, Mental Philosophy, Logic, Rhetoric, Evidence of Christianity, Elements of Criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is very broad, spanning advanced natural sciences, mathematics, the humanities, and religious instruction. The accompanying commentary in the text argues this is an extremely heavy and perhaps unrealistic examination load for a single teacher, and implies many communities would not require strict mastery of every listed subject. The phrase 'or others, the study of which would furnish an equal amount of mental discipline' suggests substitutions are acceptable if equivalent rigor is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper pedagogy for experimental sciences (critique of rote teaching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching experimental sciences (example: Chemistry) should involve actual experiments and not be limited to vague description and rote memorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes practices where 'Chemistry--think of it, ye brethren of the retort!--without experiments!!' is 'passed off on children' in expensive schools: 'For just such atrocious and ridiculous humbug have we known to be passed off on children... by vague description and by rote.' The commentary emphasizes that honest teaching of subjects like Chemistry requires months or years of additional work and, implicitly, practical demonstration; avoid purely descriptive/rote instruction for experimental sciences.
